name: Treaty with the Potawatomi, April 22, 1836 (O-kah-mause, Kee-waw-nay, Nee-boash and Mat-chis-jaw's bands)
promises: The bands ceded ten sections of land reserved for them by the second article of the Tippecanoe River treaty of October 1832 (Article 1).
The United States was to pay the bands $6,400 at the first annuity payment after ratification (Article 2).
The bands agreed to remove west of the Mississippi to the country provided for the Potawatomi within two years (Article 3); the Senate struck Article 4.
compensation: $6,400 under Article 2. Whether it was paid was not traced.
today: A 1972 dissent in the Potawatomi land claims (Dockets 29-D and 29-E) lists this treaty among thirteen made between December 1834 and February 1837 with Wabash Potawatomi village bands for village areas reserved to them in 1832, and says the reserves ceded under them were not tribal lands. No Commission award for these reserves was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's Cultural Heritage Center says federal agent Abel C. Pepper, the commissioner on this treaty, gave whiskey to young leaders to secure the village treaties of 1834 to 1837, and that the government appointed young men as chiefs when the old leaders refused to negotiate.

openQuestions: Royce gives this cession no map area (boundaries not ascertained), so nothing is drawn.
The Citizen Potawatomi Nation's account concerns the 1834 to 1837 village treaties as a group and does not name this one; it is recorded as the nation's voice, not as a breach.
The dissent was read; the majority opinion in Dockets 29-D and 29-E was not.
Which present-day nations descend from these four bands was not settled; both nations named are successors to the Potawatomi who removed west.
